title: Review: Prokaryotic cells and viruses; Cell fractionation and ultracentrifugation; The cell cycle and mitosis
source: Questions copied unchanged from the mission-lesson scripts for AQA A-level Biology (status of the source: mission-lesson scripts of Oct-Nov 2026 (reviewed by AI reviewers; not signed off by a person)). Terms and clues: CE04b#t2 term and clue written for the game; CE04b#t4 term and clue written for the game; CE06#t4 term and clue written for the game; CE06#t2 term and clue written for the game. Questions: CD01a#N.8, CE04b#N.2a, CE06#N.3, CD01a#N.11, CE04b#N.5, CE06#N.7, CD01a#N.6a, CE04b#N.7, CD01a#N.4, CD01a#N.10. Some questions repeat from the worlds it reviews.

assemble.prompt: Match each term to its definition.

items.label: Bacteriophage
items.clue: Virus with DNA in a protein head and a protein tail that injects the DNA

items.label: Acellular
items.clue: Having no cytoplasm and no ribosomes, as is true of every virus particle

items.label: Differential centrifugation
items.clue: Repeated spinning, faster and longer each time, to bring down ever smaller organelles

items.label: Isotonic
items.clue: Having the same water potential as the tissue, so organelles neither burst nor shrivel

questions.stem: A body cell has 4 chromosomes. It is in anaphase of mitosis. What is moving towards each pole of the cell?

options.text: Two whole chromosomes, each still made of two joined chromatids
Four chromatids: one sister chromatid from each of the 4 chromosomes
One chromosome from each matching (homologous) pair, chromatids still joined
Half of the cell's DNA, which each new cell will replicate after division

questions.explanation: Every chromosome splits at its centromere, and one sister chromatid goes to each pole. Each pole gets a complete, identical set of 4.

questions.stem: Which feature is shared by all viruses?

options.text: A capsid of protein enclosing either DNA or RNA, but not both
A cytoplasm in which the virus carries out metabolism
A membrane of phospholipid forming the outermost layer
A genome of DNA together with RNA, as in any living cell

questions.explanation: The few features common to all viruses are a small, fixed size; nucleic acid, either DNA or RNA, as genetic material; a capsid made of protein; no cytoplasm; and few or no enzymes. No virus contains both DNA and RNA as its genetic material.

questions.stem: Liver tissue is homogenised in an ice-cold, isotonic, buffered solution. Why must the solution be isotonic?

options.text: So the liver cells do not burst before the organelles can be collected.
So that enzymes released from the cells are denatured and cannot digest the organelles.
So that the pH of the homogenate stays constant while the organelles are being separated.
So organelles do not gain or lose water by osmosis, and do not burst or shrivel.

questions.explanation: With equal water potential inside and outside, there is no net movement of water, so the organelles keep their structure.

questions.stem: A population of a hypothetical freshwater plant reproduces only by fragmentation: pieces break off a parent plant and grow into new plants by mitosis. Which claim about the new plants is best supported?

options.text: They carry the same genetic information as the parent, except for any rare new mutations.
They can differ genetically from one another, as each mitotic division mixes up genes.
They may inherit features that the parent developed during its life, such as insect damage.
They each carry only part of the parent's genes, as each fragment receives only some.

questions.stem: A newly discovered particle 30 nm across contains one molecule of single-stranded RNA inside a protein shell. It has no ribosomes and it multiplies only inside living cells. How does the particle multiply?

options.text: It grows to about twice its size inside the cell and then divides into two identical particles.
Its RNA and proteins are made by the host cell's machinery and then assembled into new particles.
It absorbs nutrients from the cell into its cytoplasm and metabolises them to build copies of itself.
It must first acquire a DNA molecule, because one RNA strand cannot act as genetic material.

questions.stem: Which conclusion do the data support?

options.text: Most mitochondria are in pellet 2, but pellet 2 is not a pure sample of mitochondria.
Pellet 1 contains nuclei and nothing else.
Mitochondria are the densest organelles, as they are found in the first pellet.
Ribosomes are larger than mitochondria, as they need the fastest spin to be collected.

questions.explanation: Pellet 2 holds 84% of the mitochondrial enzyme, but also 5% of the DNA and 6% of the rRNA, so some nuclear material and ribosomes are mixed in.

questions.stem: Which statement correctly gives the sequence of phases in the cell cycle?

options.text: Interphase, made up of G1 and G2, is followed by S, in which the DNA is replicated, and then by mitosis and cytokinesis.
Interphase, made up of G1, S and G2 in that order, is followed by mitosis and then by cytokinesis.
Interphase, a resting period in which the cell is inactive, is followed by mitosis and then by cytokinesis.
Mitosis, which occupies most of the cycle, is followed by cytokinesis and then by a short interphase of G1, S and G2.

questions.explanation: G1, S and G2 are the stages of interphase; then mitosis, then cytokinesis. The daughter cells then enter G1 of the next cycle.

questions.stem: Bacteriophage lambda does not multiply in a sterile nutrient broth containing amino acids, nucleotides and ATP, but does multiply when living E. coli cells are added to the broth. Which explanation is correct?

options.text: The phage's own enzymes and ribosomes work only once they are activated inside a cell's cytoplasm.
The phage lacks ribosomes and most enzymes, so it needs a cell's protein synthesis machinery.
The phage cannot absorb dissolved nutrients from the broth, but it can feed on the contents of a cell.
The phage has to attach to a cell wall before it can grow large enough to divide in two.

questions.stem: A cell of an organism has 8 chromosomes before its DNA is replicated. How many chromosomes and how many DNA molecules are in its nucleus at metaphase of mitosis?

options.text: 16 chromosomes, 16 DNA molecules
8 chromosomes, 8 DNA molecules
16 chromosomes, 32 molecules of DNA
8 chromosomes, 16 DNA molecules

questions.explanation: Replication gives each of the 8 chromosomes two chromatids, each a DNA molecule: 16 DNA molecules. The chromatids stay joined until anaphase, so there are still 8 chromosomes.

questions.stem: A dividing cell is examined after its two new nuclei have formed. Many small vesicles are seen gathering and fusing in a line across the equator of the cell, midway between the nuclei. Which conclusion is justified?

options.text: It is a plant cell: the vesicles are assembling sections of new membrane and cell wall to separate the daughter cells.
It is a plant cell: the vesicles mark the line along which the cell membrane will be pinched inwards to split the cytoplasm.
It is a plant cell: the vesicles carry enzymes that soften the existing wall so that it can grow inwards across the cell.
It is an animal cell: the vesicles are new organelles that have been made from scratch so that each daughter cell has a full set.
